extracted.intended_audience: writers and philosophers preparing philosophical essays or periodical works; literary authors considering publication and style
extracted.subtask_description: Advice and evaluative criteria for composing and publishing philosophical essays and periodical literature, covering language/terminology, rhetorical strategy when truth is dangerous, attribution, and practical publishing choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Systematic philosophy must go beyond mere history/classification
rubrics_metrics.description: Is a system of philosophy, as different from mere history and historic classification possible? If possible, what are its necessary conditions? — The scheme taken with all its consequences and cleared of all inconsistencies was not less impracticable than contra-natural.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A genuine philosophical system must do more than collect and classify historical doctrines; it requires the necessary presuppositions that make speculative thought possible (not merely observational compilation). Avoid treating 'philosophy' as only a history of opinions; insist on the internal conditions and principles that constitute a system.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convey complex or dangerous truths mythically or equivocally when necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: Questions which cannot be fully answered without exposing the respondent to personal danger... the philosopher who cannot utter the whole truth without conveying falsehood, and at the same time, perhaps, exciting the most malignant passions, is constrained to express himself either mythically or equivocally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When full disclosure would mislead, harm, or expose the author (or audience) to danger, prefer symbolic, mythical, or equivocal modes of expression. Prioritize the intention of communicating truth even if that requires partial or figurative speech; recognize this as a legitimate rhetorical strategy rather than dishonesty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid pedantry: use words suitable to time, place, and company
rubrics_metrics.description: Pedantry consists in the use of words unsuitable to the time, place, and company. The mere man of the world, who insists that no other terms but such as occur in common conversation should be employed in a scientific disquisition, is as truly a pedant as the man of letters who over-rates the acquirements of his auditors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose diction appropriate to your audience and occasion. Pedantry is not only the scholar's ostentation but also the layman's crude insistence on colloquialism; both are faults. Balance precision with accessibility; avoid using terminology that alienates or confuses readers unnecessarily.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer introducing new technical terms rather than reusing old words with new meanings
rubrics_metrics.description: The instructor has no other alternative than either to use old words with new meanings (the plan adopted by Darwin in his Zoonomia), or to introduce new terms... The latter mode is evidently preferable, only that the former demands a twofold exertion of thought in one and the same act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a concept needs a distinct meaning, coin a new term rather than overloading an existing one — reusing an old word forces the reader to unlearn the habitual meaning and learn the new one simultaneously. New terms reduce confusion, though they impose the cost of learning vocabulary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer restoring obsolete appropriate terms over coining entirely new ones
rubrics_metrics.description: Where indeed, it is in our power to recall an appropriate term that had without sufficient reason become obsolete, it is doubtless a less evil to restore than to coin anew.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an older term exactly fits a needed concept (and has fallen out of use), consider reviving it rather than inventing a neologism. This can aid comprehension and conserve linguistic economy; example given: adopting 'sensuous' for passive perception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wean attention from degrees to kinds: focus on abstract kinds in philosophical discourse
rubrics_metrics.description: The first lesson of philosophic discipline is to wean the student's attention from the degrees of things, which alone form the vocabulary of common life, and to direct it to the kind abstracted from degree.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Philosophical analysis should prioritise distinctions of kind and essential categories over merely gradational or quantitative descriptions. Train readers (and students) to think in terms of conceptual kinds rather than only in degrees or intensities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Similarity of thought or phrase is not definitive proof of borrowing; attribute when possible and explain limits
rubrics_metrics.description: An identity of thought, or even similarity of phrase will not be at all times a certain proof that the passage has been borrowed from [another author]... For readers in general, let whatever shall be found in this or any future work of mine that resembles, or coincides with, the doctrines of my German predecessor, though contemporary, be wholly attributed to him; provided... the absence of distinct references... be not charged on me as an ungenerous concealment or intentional plagiarism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When parallels occur, acknowledge them where you can, but recognise independent convergence of ideas. Where citations cannot be made (lack of access to sources), state the limitation openly to avoid appearing as intentional concealment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not trust subscription numbers as reliable indicators of sustained readership
rubrics_metrics.description: I warn him, in the first place, against trusting in the number of names on his subscription list... Of these hundred patrons ninety threw up the publication before the fourth number, without any notice; though it was well known to them...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat subscription lists and early pledges cautiously — they may be unreliable and not translate into continued support or payment. Plan finances and print runs with an expectation of attrition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid uniting the functions of author and publisher; consider selling copyright
rubrics_metrics.description: I warn all others from the attempt to deviate from the ordinary mode of publishing a work by the trade... it is hard... then after all to give thirty per cent... to a man who has merely to give the books shelf or warehouse room... Yet even this is better... than to attempt in any way to unite the functions of author and publisher. But the most prudent mode is to sell the copyright...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Self-publishing imposes extra costs, logistical burdens, and anxieties; authors are often better served by using established trade publishing (even at the cost of a share of receipts) or by selling copyright for an edition to secure immediate payment and peace of mind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accept trade customs pragmatically; avoid moralising about booksellers' practices
rubrics_metrics.description: The individuals did not make the laws and customs of their trade... Till the evil can be proved to be removable and without the substitution of an equal or greater inconvenience, it were neither wise nor manly even to complain of it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When dealing with publishing trades, be pragmatic. Recognise commercial norms and work within them rather than denouncing practitioners individually; focus on feasible reforms rather than indignation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate unlearned or mystical writers by substance not superficial polish
rubrics_metrics.description: It would not be easy to discover any substantial ground for this contemptuous pride in those literati... unless it be that they could write orthographically, make smooth periods... while the latter, in simplicity of soul, made their words immediate echoes of their feelings... there exist folios on the human understanding which would have a far juster claim to their high rank... if in the whole huge volume there could be found as much fulness of heart and intellect as burst forth in many a simple page of George Fox, Jacob Behmen...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not dismiss writings from the unlearned or mystics merely because they lack scholastic polish. Assess for 'fulness of heart and intellect' — the genuine insight can lie beneath rough form; readers may need superior discernment to extract meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and reintroduce precise technical distinctions (e.g., sensuous; objective/subjective)
rubrics_metrics.description: To express in one word all that appertains to the perception considered as passive, and merely recipient, I have adopted from our elder classics the word sensuous... Thus too I have followed Hooker, Sanderson, Milton, &c. in designating the immediateness of any act or object of knowledge by the word immediate... The very words, objective and subjective... I have ventured to re-introduce.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When nuance demands, adopt or revive precise technical vocabulary (objective/subjective, sensuous, immediate). Careful terminological choices reduce ambiguity in philosophical writing; prefer established technical terms if they aid clarity.
